"You look at problems through one lens. Many computations are a loop: the next state is computed from the current one,
so step 1,000 cannot start until step 999 ends, and when the state is small most of a GPU sits idle. Such a loop can
sometimes be computed all at once: guess every state, check every step in parallel against the one before, correct
all the errors together, and repeat until nothing changes. The result is exactly what the loop would give. It pays only
when the system forgets its past, so that early errors fade: damped, dissipative or mixing dynamics, or a long sampling
chain. It fails when small errors grow, as in chaotic systems. Before spending, measure forgetfulness: start two runs a
hair apart and see whether they converge or drift apart. A good candidate has a step-by-step loop, a small state (a
handful to a few hundred numbers), a long run (thousands of steps or more), forgetful dynamics, and few runs needed; if
thousands of runs are needed, run them side by side instead. The method does more total arithmetic and wins only on how
long one answer takes. Before proposing anything, check whether a strong GPU method for this already exists; rebuilding
it wins nothing. Write down your predictions and how you could be wrong before any test, and compare against a tuned
sequential baseline and against many independent copies run side by side.

Here is a research problem as it was first written down, with the question it belongs to.
Root question: What's actually stopping general purpose robot hands from reliably doing stuff like folding laundry or loading a dishwasher? Is it the lack of real-world manipulation data, the hardware (sensors, actuators, tactile feedback), or the sim-to-real gap? Is that a major blocker at some level, and could it be fixed by running millions of simulated robots in parallel on a shit ton of GPUs?
Problem:
Inference-time steering of VLA internals (SAEs, FFN vectors, conceptors, linear observers)
Steering a VLA's internal features can bring out behaviour the model already has, without retraining. On real DROID hardware, SAE steering of pi0.5 raised target-object grasps by +9 to +21 out of 25 trials, and ablating the top-4 general features cut success from 39/40 to 0/40. COAST conceptors raised pi0.5 on LIBERO-10 from 0.43 to 0.80, with about +40% on three real tasks. Grant et al. found motor programs bound to absolute coordinates (50/50 grasps at the recorded spot on a UR10e). All tests are rigid tabletop tasks; none is cloth or a dish rack. Goodfire markets steering for robotics but publishes no numbers.
What more compute would buy: The quantity is closed-loop rollouts and SAEs swept; the largest is 420,000+ rollouts and 520+ SAEs across six VLAs (https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.19233), and above that it is unknown whether any feature controls contact-rich or deformable behaviour, because every sweep so far ran rigid pick-and-place or drawer tasks.
What runs step after step: Each feature waits on an SAE fit (about 6,700 Adam steps, derived from https://arxiv.org/html/2603.19183; 'a few GPU-hours per SAE on one A100') and then on closed-loop rollouts of up to 300 steps, each waiting on a ~150 ms VLA forward pass and the next observation; the answer needed 150 rollouts × 135 features (20,250 episodes), and one unbatched rollout leaves the GPU idle while the simulator steps. Steps within a rollout must run in order, but rollouts are independent: batching hundreds of steered environments in a GPU-parallel simulator, with a separate hook per environment and simulation pipelined against inference, would run them together; this pays only if steering effects in simulation match the real robot (false for cloth). The nearest attempt is RLinf-VLA, 1.61-1.88x with 256 ManiSkill environments, for RL rather than interpretability (https://arxiv.org/html/2510.06710v2).

Find where this problem stops more compute from helping, or where more compute only buys more of the same. Then look for reframings: changes to what is measured, the unit of work, the objective or the order of steps that would let more compute change the answer. Give up to three. End each with one question someone could investigate: specific, answerable by a measurement, and naming what is measured. For each, give the cheapest measurement that would answer it or show it is not worth pursuing, with a rough cost. Decide from the text above and what you know; do not use tools.

Return only one JSON value, with no other text, that matches this JSON Schema:
{\"type\":\"object\",\"required\":[\"reframes\"],\"properties\":{\"reframes\":{\"type\":\"array\",\"items\":{\"type\":\"object\",\"required\":[\"bottleneck\",\"assumption\",\"reframe\",\"question\",\"measure\",\"compute_after\",\"exact\",\"expected\",\"fails_if\",\"closest_prior\"],\"properties\":{\"bottleneck\":{\"type\":\"string\"},\"assumption\":{\"type\":\"string\"},\"reframe\":{\"type\":\"string\"},\"question\":{\"type\":\"string\"},\"measure\":{\"type\":\"string\"},\"compute_after\":{\"type\":\"string\"},\"exact\":{\"type\":\"string\"},\"expected\":{\"type\":\"string\"},\"fails_if\":{\"type\":\"string\"},\"closest_prior\":{\"type\":\"string\"}}}}}}"

Let me carefully analyze this task. I'm given a research problem about inference-time steering of VLA (Vision-Language-Action) internals for robotics. The context includes a framing about parallel-in-time methods (the first paragraph describes methods like Parareal, parallel-in-time integration, which work when dynamics are "forgetful" — damped, dissipative, mixing — and fail for chaotic systems).

The task: Find where this problem stops more compute from helping, or where more compute only buys more of the same. Then look for reframings: changes to what is measured, the unit of work, the objective, or the order of steps that would let more compute change the answer. Give up to three. End each with one question someone could investigate: specific, answerable by a measurement, naming what is measured. For each, give the cheapest measurement that would answer it or show it is not worth pursuing, with a rough cost.

The JSON schema requires for each reframe:
- bottleneck: where the problem stops more compute from helping
- assumption: the assumption underlying the bottleneck
- reframe: the reframing
- question: specific, answerable by measurement, naming what is measured
- measure: cheapest measurement with rough cost
- compute_after: what compute buys after the reframe
- exact: exact specification of the measurement
- expected: expected outcome
- fails_if: what would show it's not worth pursuing
- closest_prior: closest prior work

Let me think about the problem deeply.

The problem: Steering VLA internals (SAEs, conceptors, etc.) works for rigid tabletop tasks. The unknown: whether any feature controls contact-rich or deformable behaviour (cloth folding, dish loading), because every sweep so far ran rigid pick-and-place or drawer tasks. Compute currently spent: 420k+ rollouts, 520+ SAEs across six VLAs. Each SAE costs ~6,700 Adam steps, a few GPU-hours on A100. Rollouts: up to 300 steps, each step waits on ~150ms VLA forward pass + observation; 20,250 episodes for one answer. Rollouts are independent and can be batched in GPU-parallel simulators (RLinf-VLA got 1.61-1.88x with 256 ManiSkill envs).

Key bottlenecks where more compute stops helping:

1. **The sim-to-real gap for deformables**: the text says "this pays only if steering effects in simulation match the real robot (false for cloth)". So more compute on simulation rollouts for cloth buys nothing if sim cloth doesn't transfer. The bottleneck is not rollout throughput but the fidelity/transfer of the measured quantity. Reframe: change what is measured — instead of measuring steering success in sim, measure the steering effect direction/magnitude transfer coefficient between sim and real on a small set of paired trials; or measure on real robot directly with cheap proxy tasks. The unit of work could change from "full task success episodes" to "single-step or few-step perturbation response" measurements which are cheaper and can be done on real hardware.

2. **Feature discovery objective**: Current approach sweeps SAEs trained on activations from rigid tasks; the assumption is that features for contact-rich/deformable behavior exist in the model and can be found by the same SAE training distribution. If the model was rarely shown cloth/deformable interactions, the features may not exist — more SAE training compute only buys more of the same rigid-task features. Reframe: change the objective — train SAEs on activations collected during contact-rich/deformable episodes (even failed ones), or change what is measured: measure feature-level variance/causal effect in contact-rich data vs rigid. Question: does the causal effect size of top features differ when SAE is fit on contact-rich activations vs pooled? Cheapest measurement: collect a few hundred contact-rich episodes (teleop or scripted, in sim or real), fit one SAE on that activation subset, ablate top features, measure success change on a contact-rich probe task. Cost: maybe ~$2-5k or a few hundred GPU-hours plus robot hours.

3. **Order of steps**: Currently: fit SAE (6,700 steps), then run closed-loop rollouts per feature. The rollout sweep is the expensive part (150 rollouts × 135 features). Reframe: screen features with cheap open-loop / single-step probes before paying for closed-loop rollouts — change the order so compute is allocated hierarchically: measure one-step action divergence under feature ablation/steering on a fixed state set, rank features, then closed-loop only top-k. Question: does single-step action-delta rank correlate with closed-loop success delta rank? Measurement: for ~135 features, compute steering-induced action changes on ~1,000 recorded states (batched forward passes, ~hours), compare ranking to existing closed-loop results (already computed for some tasks, e.g., pi0.5 LIBERO). Cost: tens of GPU-hours.

4. **Forgetfulness/parallel-in-time angle** (connecting to the first paragraph): The rollouts are sequential 300-step loops; the intro text suggests parallel-in-time methods pay when dynamics forget. Contact-rich manipulation with friction/contact is often dissipative (in-hand sliding settles, cloth is damped) — but the VLA policy closed loop may be chaotic? Actually a reframing: treat closed-loop rollout as a fixed-point/parallel-in-time problem — guess all observations/actions, check consistency in parallel. But the observation depends on the simulator state, which is the long sequential chain. Hmm, the sim dynamics are deterministic given state+action; parallel-in-time for rigid body sim with contact... contact dynamics are often dissipative (damped), so maybe parallel-in-time works for cloth (heavily damped, forgetful — errors in cloth configuration decay as it settles under gravity/damping). That's an interesting reframe of the unit of work: instead of stepping the simulator sequentially per rollout, solve the whole trajectory at once. But the policy forward pass depends on observations which depend on state... the whole loop could be guessed and checked. Actually the big win: the measurement question — measure Lyapunov exponent / perturbation decay of the closed-loop system: start two simulations a hair apart, see if they converge. For cloth tasks, likely converges (damped). Then parallel-in-time could replace sequential stepping. But is that where the bottleneck is? The text says rollouts are independent and batchable — RLinf-VLA already gets speedup. So the sequential-in-time bottleneck is already addressed by batching; parallel-in-time adds more only if single-rollout latency matters (it does for real-robot rollouts where you can't batch beyond available robots!). On real hardware, each rollout is 300 steps × 150ms+ and you can't parallelize time on one robot. Hmm, but parallel-in-time on real hardware is impossible since the real world doesn't let you guess-and-check states. In sim, you can.

Let me structure three reframes:

**Reframe 1 — Change what is measured: from task success in sim to transfer coefficient of steering effects.**
- Bottleneck: For cloth/deformable tasks, more sim rollouts buy nothing because steering effects measured in sim may not match real robot ("false for cloth"); compute only buys more of the same (rigid-task evidence).
- Assumption: The quantity being measured (sim closed-loop success under steering) is a proxy for the quantity wanted (real-robot success under steering).
- Reframe: Measure the sim→real transfer of the *steering effect* (the delta caused by a feature), not the task success itself. The delta may transfer even when absolute success doesn't, because it is a difference that cancels sim bias. Change the unit of work from "episode success" to "effect-size paired comparison."
- Question: Is the per-feature steering effect (change in grasp-success rate or action distribution) rank-preserved between sim and real on a contact-rich probe task? Measure Spearman correlation of per-feature effect sizes across ~20 features.
- Measure: Pick one contact-rich sim task (e.g., ManiSkill cloth or a dish-in-rack insertion) and its real twin; run 25 rollouts per feature for 20 features in sim (batched, ~few hundred GPU-hours) and 25 paired real trials per feature on one DROID setup (~2 weeks of robot time, ~$5-10k). Compute rank correlation of effect sizes.
- Compute after: If transfer holds, the full 520-SAE × 420k-rollout sweep in sim becomes informative for cloth; GPU-parallel batching then directly scales it.
- Exact: Spearman ρ between sim and real per-feature Δsuccess (or Δaction-logit on target object) across 20 features, 25 paired episodes each.
- Expected: ρ > 0.5 for rigid-adjacent contact tasks; unknown for cloth.
- Fails if: ρ ≈ 0 or negative — then sim sweeps for deformables are worthless and compute should go to real-robot data collection instead.
- Closest prior: arxiv 2603.19233 (520 SAEs, 420k rollouts sweep); RLinf-VLA for batched rollouts; sim-to-real transfer studies of policy deltas.

**Reframe 2 — Change the order of steps: cheap single-step screening before expensive closed-loop rollouts.**
- Bottleneck: The expensive unit is the closed-loop rollout (300 sequential steps × 150 ms, repeated 150×135); most features have no effect, so most rollout compute is spent confirming zeros. More compute only buys more zeros faster.
- Assumption: A feature's closed-loop effect can only be measured by full closed-loop rollouts.
- Reframe: Reorder the pipeline — screen all features with a batched open-loop probe (steer/ablating and measure action divergence on a fixed bank of recorded states) and pay closed-loop rollouts only for the top-k. The unit of work changes from episode to single forward pass.
- Question: Does the open-loop steering-induced action-delta magnitude rank-order features the same as closed-loop success deltas? Measure Kendall/Spearman correlation between the two rankings on an existing benchmark where closed-loop numbers exist.
- Measure: For ~135 features on pi0.5, compute mean ||a_steered − a_base|| over ~1,000 recorded states from the 2603.19183 dataset; compare ranking against published closed-loop per-feature effects. Cost: ~1-10 GPU-hours (135 features × 1,000 states = 135k forward passes, batched) plus analysis; trivial vs the 20,250 episodes.
- Compute after: If rank correlation is high, each new sweep needs closed-loop rollouts for only ~top-10 features, cutting rollout compute ~10×, letting the same budget sweep 10× more SAEs/tasks (including contact-rich).
- Exact: Spearman ρ between per-feature mean action L2 delta (open loop, 1,000 states) and per-feature closed-loop Δsuccess (150 rollouts), across 135 features.
- Expected: ρ 0.4-0.7; action-conditioned filtering keeps all features with any closed-loop effect (recall near 1 at top-30).
- Fails if: ρ < ~0.3 — closed-loop compounding effects dominate single-step responses, screening must stay closed-loop.
- Closest prior: 2603.19233's closed-loop sweep; open-loop vs closed-loop VLA evaluation literature (open-loop action MSE notoriously mis-ranks policies — that's the risk).

**Reframe 3 — Change the objective: fit SAEs on contact-rich activations (the features may not exist in rigid-task SAEs).**
- Bottleneck: The sweep answers "does any feature control contact-rich behavior" with features found on rigid-task activations; if the relevant directions are absent/unidentified in those SAEs, more rollouts per feature only buy more of the same null result. The SAE fit itself is cheap (~few GPU-hours); the binding constraint is what data the SAE saw.
- Assumption: Features that control contact-rich/deformable behavior are present and discoverable in activations collected from rigid pick-and-place rollouts.
- Reframe: Change the SAE training distribution (the objective's data) — fit SAEs on activations from contact-rich/deformable episodes (even simulated or teleop failures), then sweep. The unit of compute shifts from rollouts-per-feature to activation collection from a new distribution.
- Question: Do SAEs fit on contact-rich activations yield features whose ablation changes contact-rich task success, where rigid-fit SAE features show none? Measure per-SAE max causal effect (ablation Δsuccess) on a contact-rich probe.
- Measure: Collect ~500 contact-rich episodes in a GPU-parallel sim (ManiSkill cloth/pegb-in-hole), ~50k-150k steps of activations (~one day on one A100); fit 2-3 SAEs (each ~6,700 Adam steps, few GPU-hours); ablate top-8 features × 25 rollouts (~200 episodes, batched ~1 GPU-day). Total order ~100 GPU-hours + ~$1k.
- Compute after: If new features appear, the whole 420k-rollout machinery finally has something to measure for cloth; scaling SAE count and rollout count changes the answer.
- Exact: Max over features of |Δsuccess| under ablation on the contact-rich probe, contact-fit SAE vs rigid-fit SAE, 25 episodes per feature, same total feature count and sparsity.
- Expected: Contact-fit SAE yields ≥1 feature with ablation Δsuccess ≥ 20 points on contact-rich task; rigid-fit shows ≤5 points (its known effects are on rigid tasks).
- Fails if: Neither SAE yields any feature with causal effect on contact-rich behavior — suggesting the VLA lacks such internal control knobs and steering compute should stop.
- Closest prior: 2603.19183 (SAE fit procedure, 6,700 Adam steps), 2603.19233 (sweep), Goodfire steering claims.

Alternatively, a third reframe about parallel-in-time for the closed-loop rollouts themselves, tying to the intro paragraph:

**Alternative Reframe — Change the unit of work from sequential rollout steps to all-at-once trajectory solve (parallel-in-time).**
- Bottleneck: Even with batched environments, each rollout's 300 steps run in order; a single unbatched rollout leaves the GPU idle, and wall-clock per answer is bounded by 300 × 150ms. RLinf-VLA gets only 1.61-1.88×. 
- Assumption: The closed-loop trajectory must be computed step-by-step.
- Reframe: Guess all observations/actions/states, check each step against the previous in parallel, iterate until consistent — pays if the closed-loop dynamics forget (cloth is damped/dissipative; the VLA policy may smooth errors). Measure forgetfulness first: perturb the sim state mid-rollout and measure divergence decay.
- Question: Do perturbed cloth-manipulation rollouts reconverge (perturbation norm halves within k steps)? Measure divergence between two runs started a hair apart at various points in the episode.
- Measure: In ManiSkill cloth task, run 64 paired rollouts with a small state perturbation injected at steps 50/100/200, log state-distance vs steps-after-perturbation; ~a few GPU-days. Fit decay rate.
- Compute after: If half-life ≪ episode length, parallel-in-time across the 300 steps multiplies batch parallelism by time parallelism (another ~10-50×), cutting wall-clock per sweep from days to hours.
- Fails if: Perturbations grow (chaotic contact, policy amplifies) — then sequential stepping is mandatory and only environment batching helps.
- Closest prior: Parareal/parallel-in-time literature; RLinf-VLA 1.61-1.88× with 256 envs.

Hmm — I have four candidates. Which three are strongest? The prompt's intro paragraph strongly hints at the forgetfulness measurement and parallel-in-time; the text itself says "Before spending, measure forgetfulness: start two runs a hair apart and see whether they converge or drift apart." So including the parallel-in-time reframe seems aligned with the intent. But the problem statement's own core unknown is "whether any feature controls contact-rich or deformable behaviour" — the data-distribution reframe (3) and the transfer reframe (1) address that directly. The screening reframe (2) is a solid order-of-steps reframe.

The task says "up to three." I should pick the three that best satisfy: "Find where this problem stops more compute from helping, or where more compute only buys more of the same." 

Let me evaluate:

1. Transfer reframe: This is the sharpest "more compute buys nothing" point — the text explicitly says "this pays only if steering effects in simulation match the real robot (false for cloth)". So all the batched-rollout compute for cloth in sim is wasted unless transfer holds. Strong.

2. Screening/order reframe: More compute currently buys mostly null results; reordering makes compute buy information. Strong and cheap to test. Good.

3. Data-distribution reframe: Addresses the core unknown directly; the sweep with rigid-fit SAEs might only ever produce nulls for cloth, so more compute = more of the same nulls. Strong.

4. Parallel-in-time reframe: Aligned with the framing paragraph; the bottleneck (150ms sequential latency, GPU idle) is real but batching largely addresses throughput; the marginal win is wall-clock per answer. It also has a clean cheap measurement (perturbation decay). The prompt's first paragraph is essentially instructions for how to think about this, and the reframe list benefits from one "unit of work"/"order of steps" mechanics reframe.

I have room for only three. Reframe 2 and 4 both concern the mechanics of rollouts. Reframe 2 (screening) probably dominates 4 in expected value: it cuts work by 10×+ at trivial cost, whereas parallel-in-time for a closed-loop VLA+simulator is technically hairy (the policy forward pass depends on observations rendered from sim states; guessing the full joint trajectory and iterating may need many fixed-point iterations, and contact-rich cloth may still be locally stiff). But the intro text explicitly primes the parallel-in-time idea, and the grader may expect one reframe along those lines. Hmm.

Actually, note: the intro paragraph is generic — it's the same "reframe" guidance given to every problem in this series (it mentions damped/dissipative/mixing dynamics, long sampling chains, small state, long runs). For this problem, rollouts are 300 steps (borderline "long"), state is a robot+scene (small-ish), and the closed-loop includes a neural policy. The forgetfulness measurement is genuinely the gating question for any parallel-in-time proposal. I think including it as one reframe, with the cheap perturbation-decay measurement, is faithful to the setup.

But wait — does parallel-in-time actually change the answer, or just speed? The task says reframings "that would let more compute change the answer." Speed alone ("wins only on how long one answer takes") is acknowledged in the intro as a valid win ("The method does more total arithmetic and wins only on how long one answer takes"). So a wall-clock reframe qualifies, but it's weaker than reframes where compute changes what's knowable (transfer, data distribution).

Decision: Go with (1) transfer, (2) screening order, (3) contact-rich SAE data. And fold the forgetfulness/parallel-in-time idea... hmm, I could merge it into reframe 2's "compute_after"? No, keep them clean.

Alternatively: (1) transfer, (3) data, (4) parallel-in-time, dropping screening? The screening reframe is very concrete and cheap with existing data — it directly addresses "more compute only buys more of the same" (150 rollouts × 135 features where most are nulls). I think screening is one of the strongest because the measurement can reuse already-published per-feature closed-loop results, costing almost nothing.

Let me weigh once more which three maximize quality per the schema:

- Transfer (sim→real of steering effect): bottleneck = the stated "false for cloth" caveat; assumption = sim success is the proxy; reframe = measure effect-transfer, a difference that cancels sim bias; question = rank correlation of per-feature deltas; cheap measure = ~20 features × 25 paired episodes in sim and on one real setup. Cost: sim side ~ a few hundred GPU-hours batched; real side ~100-200 robot-hours. This is the gating measurement for all further cloth compute. Strongest.

- Screening (open-loop probe before closed-loop): bottleneck = compute spent confirming nulls; assumption = closed-loop rollouts are the only way to rank features; reframe = order of steps; question = rank correlation between open-loop action delta and closed-loop success delta; measure = ~135 features × 1k states batched forward passes, compare to published rankings; cost ~ single-digit GPU-hours plus analysis. Very cheap, decisive.

- Data distribution (fit SAEs on contact-rich activations): bottleneck = the answer "no feature controls cloth" may be an artifact of where features were looked for; assumption = features exist in rigid-task SAE dictionaries; reframe = change objective/data; question = does a contact-fit SAE contain causally effective features for a contact-rich probe where a rigid-fit SAE has none; measure = collect ~50k contact-rich activation steps in batched sim, fit 2 SAEs (~10 GPU-hours each), ablate top-8 × 25 episodes; total ~100 GPU-hours. 

I'll go with these three. But let me reconsider including parallel-in-time instead of one of them... The instructions: "Find where this problem stops more compute from helping, or where more compute only buys more of the same. Then look for reframings: changes to what is measured, the unit of work, the objective or the order of steps." 

- Transfer = change in what is measured. ✓
- Screening = change in order of steps. ✓
- Data = change in objective (what the SAE optimizes to represent). ✓
- Parallel-in-time = change in unit of work. ✓

Nice coverage would include a unit-of-work reframe. Screening is "order of steps"; data is "objective"; transfer is "what is measured". The unit-of-work slot would be filled by parallel-in-time (episode → whole trajectory solved at once) or by the screening (episode → single forward pass, which is arguably unit-of-work too). I can frame screening as both order and unit-of-work. I'll keep my three and note the unit change within screening. Actually, to honor the intro paragraph's explicit instruction ("Before spending, measure forgetfulness..."), I could fold the forgetfulness measurement into the screening reframe's compute_after? No — keep it clean.

Hmm, let me reconsider once more. The intro text says "It fails when small errors grow, as in chaotic systems. Before spending, measure forgetfulness." If I include parallel-in-time as a reframe, the measurement is exactly the one prescribed. The problem text says "Steps within a rollout must run in order, but rollouts are independent: batching... would run them together" and cites RLinf-VLA's 1.61-1.88×. The modest 1.61-1.88× suggests batching alone underdelivers (why only 1.61-1.88×? probably simulator/inference pipeline overheads). A parallel-in-time reframe would target the residual sequential latency. But honestly, for the scientific question ("does any feature control cloth behavior?"), throughput is not the binding constraint — transfer and feature existence are. The problem statement itself asks "What more compute would buy" and flags the sim-real match as the condition. So the three I chose map onto the real blockers. I'll mention parallel-in-time as closest_prior context? No, keep closest_prior accurate for each.

Actually, I realize I can satisfy the intro-paragraph nod inside reframe 2 or as part of the "compute_after" of the transfer reframe... Not needed. Three clean reframes.

Wait, one more consideration on the "question" requirement: "specific, answerable by a measurement, and naming what is measured." Each question must name the measured quantity. Let me draft:

R1 question: "Is the per-feature steering effect size (Δ in target-grasp success vs baseline) rank-correlated between a GPU-parallel simulator and the real robot on a contact-rich task, measured as Spearman ρ across ≥20 features × 25 paired episodes?"

R2 question: "Does the open-loop steering response — mean L2 change in the action chunk when a feature is clamped, measured over 1,000 recorded states — rank the 135 features the same as their closed-loop Δsuccess (Spearman ρ between the two rankings)?"

R3 question: "Does an SAE fit on contact-rich activations contain any feature whose ablation changes contact-rich task success by ≥20 points, where a rigid-fit SAE's max effect is ≤5 points, measured as per-feature Δsuccess over 25 episodes per feature?"

Now the fields:

- bottleneck: concise statement.
- assumption: the hidden assumption.
- reframe: what changes.
- question: as above.
- measure: cheapest measurement + rough cost.
- compute_after: what more compute buys if the measurement comes out positive.
- exact: the exact protocol/numbers.
- expected: expected result with reasoning.
- fails_if: the kill criterion.
- closest_prior: nearest prior work from the text or known literature.

Costs: let me be realistic.
- R1: sim side: 20 features × 25 episodes × 300 steps × 150ms ≈ 20×25×45s = 6.25 h of sequential rollout, batched across 256 envs → minutes-to-hours of wall-clock on one node; call it ~50 GPU-hours with overhead. Real side: 500 episodes × ~2 min ≈ 17 robot-hours plus resets; realistically 1-2 weeks of one DROID setup, a few thousand dollars. Total order $5k. Cheapest version: reuse the 3 real tasks from COAST (they report ~+40% on three real tasks) — maybe measure transfer on rigid tasks first for ~$0 using published paired numbers? Actually a near-free version: compute Spearman between sim LIBERO numbers and the reported real-task numbers from COAST across the conceptors/features already published. That's cheap but coarse (few features). The cheap decisive version: 10-20 features, one sim task + its real twin. I'll give cost ~1-2 weeks robot time + ~100 GPU-hours, ≈ $3-8k.

- R2: 135 features × 1,000 states = 135k steered forward passes; batched at ~100/s on one A100 → ~30-60 min; total <10 GPU-hours; comparison to published closed-loop effects is free. Cost ~$20-50. 

- R3: collect 500 contact-rich episodes in batched ManiSkill (256 envs, ~hours) → activations for ~150k steps; fit 2-3 SAEs at few GPU-hours each (~10-20 GPU-hours); ablation sweep 8 features × 25 episodes × 2 SAEs = 400 episodes batched → ~1 GPU-day. Total ~50-100 GPU-hours, ~$200-500. No real robot needed for the first pass.

Closest priors:
- R1: the pi0.5 SAE steering real-robot numbers (DROID hardware, +9..+21/25) and COAST's sim-vs-real gap (0.43→0.80 LIBERO, +40% real); sim-to-real transfer literature; RLinf-VLA for the batched sim side. Also 2603.19233.
- R2: open-loop vs closed-loop evaluation findings in VLA literature (open-loop action error mis-ranks closed-loop success — reported in several VLA papers); 2603.19233 sweep; the single-step probe resembles feature-attribution/activation patching screens.
- R3: 2603.19183 SAE training recipe; SAE-on-robotics work (Goodfire); Grant et al. motor programs; the pi0.5 ablation (39/40→0/40) as evidence features can be causal.

Let me also make sure "compute_after" states what the bigger compute would buy once the gate passes:
